title: Control Expiration Dates & Shelf Life — Shift Leader Walk
description:
Controlling expiration dates and shelf life is one of the brand's Big 6 areas of food safety risk. This walk is about that one thing.

It starts at our own make table, then you finish it standing in your walk-in with the door open. Nothing here is a memory test — the dates are in front of you. Read the labels.

questions.title: It is Monday 11/16. Tap each label to read it, then tap the one product that has to come out of this table.

hotspots.label: The bacon — Discard Sun 11/15 Close, and it is Monday
hotspots.why: Its discard day was last night at close. It should never have made it to this shift.

questions.help: This is our own make table. Our labels read Made, Ready and Discard.
questions.explanation:
The bacon. Its label says Discard Sun 11/15 Close, and it is Monday morning.

• The Italian sausage says Mon 11/16 Close. That is today, so it is fine right now — it comes out tonight at close, not now.
• Pepperoni and diced ham are both still days out.
• Only the bacon is already past, and it is past by one night.

This is the one that catches stores out. Nobody pulled it at close, it is still sitting there in the morning, and now it is a deviation. Dated product gets pulled at close, not at open.

questions.title: A case of diced tomatoes in the walk-in has the manufacturer's date printed on the bag. You find one bag a single day past that date. What does that score?
choices: Nothing — one day past is still inside the window
A Secondary deviation
A Significant deviation
Nothing, as long as the bag is still sealed
questions.explanation:
Significant. There is no grace day — one day past is past.

• A TCS product past the manufacturer's date is the most serious finding in this whole section.
• A Significant deviation has to be remediated within 24 hours.
• Still sealed rescues nothing. Unopened and out of date is still out of date.

This is not hypothetical. An auditor found exactly this in one of our walk-ins: diced tomatoes, expiration date 06/13, found on 06/14. One day. Scored Significant.

questions.title: In the same walk-in, a tub of Alfredo that we opened and date-marked ourselves is two days past the date we wrote on it. What does that score?
choices: A Significant deviation, the same as the tomatoes
A Secondary deviation
Nothing — we wrote the date, so we can extend it
Nothing, because it is not a manufacturer's date
questions.explanation:
Secondary. Whose date it is changes how hard it hits.

• Manufacturer's date past — Significant.
• Our own date-mark past — Secondary.
• An opened item with no date on it at all — also Secondary, and just as avoidable.

Both of these came off the same cooler on the same day: the tomatoes scored Significant, the Alfredo scored Secondary. Same shelf, same visit, different severity.

The Secondary line is the one that is entirely ours. It is fixed with a marker.

questions.title: A bag has two dates printed on it: "Sell By 11/20" and "Best By 11/28". Which one is the expiration date for the audit?
choices: Best By 11/28 — it is the latest one
Sell By 11/20 — it is the earliest one
Neither — only a date that says "Expiration" counts
Whichever one the manufacturer says is the real one
questions.explanation:
The earliest date on the packaging, whatever it is called.

• "Best By", "Use By", "Expiration", "Sell By" — they all count.
• The earliest one wins. This bag is out of date after 11/20, not 11/28.

Reading for the latest date on a bag is how a product sits in the cooler looking legal for another week.

questions.title: Which of these would cost us points? Pick ALL that apply.
choices: A sealed bag of a TCS product with no manufacturer's expiration date printed on it anywhere
An opened bag of sauce in the walk-in with no date written on it
A tub we prepped three days ago, labeled, still inside its date
A case of a TCS product past the manufacturer's date, still sealed
An opened, date-marked container that is past the date we wrote on it
questions.explanation:
Four of these five score against us.

• No manufacturer's date on a TCS product — Significant. A missing date is treated as seriously as a passed one.
• Opened with no date written on it — Secondary.
• Sealed but past the manufacturer's date — Significant.
• Past our own date-mark — Secondary.

The prepped tub, labeled and still in date, is the only one that is right. That is what good looks like, and it took somebody ten seconds with a marker.

questions.title: You open a bag of a ready-to-eat TCS product and put it in the walk-in. You are going to hold it longer than 24 hours. What has to happen?
choices: Nothing — the manufacturer's date on the bag still covers it
It gets labeled, and served or thrown out within 7 days
It gets labeled, and served or thrown out within 14 days
It has to be used by the end of the next day
questions.explanation:
Labeled, then served or discarded within 7 days.

• Opening it starts a second clock. The bag's own date is no longer the only one running.
• Ready-to-eat, TCS, staying more than 24 hours — it needs our label on it.
• Seven days is the outer limit, not a target.

Plenty of products are shorter than seven days. Look at our own make table: the buttery sauce is made Wednesday and discarded Thursday at close. One day. Check Pizzapedia for the item in your hand rather than defaulting everything to seven.

questions.title: It is 4pm. You find a product whose discard date is today. What do you do?
choices: Throw it out right now — it is already expired
It is good through close of business today, then it is discarded
It is good until this time tomorrow
Mark it down and use it first
questions.explanation:
Good through close of business, then discarded.

• The date on the label is the last day you can use it, not the first day it is bad.
• That is why our labels say "Close" — Discard Thu 10/22 Close means it goes at close on Thursday.

Throwing it out at 4pm is waste. Leaving it for tomorrow is a deviation. The label already tells you exactly when, and somebody has to actually do it.

questions.title: You just found product that is past date. What do you do? Pick everything that applies.
choices: Pull it out of the walk-in now, not at the end of the shift
Tell your manager
Check the rest of that product and anything stored beside it
Use it today and order fresh for tomorrow
Look at why it was missed — whether it was rotation, labeling or over-ordering
questions.explanation:
Pull it, say something, check around it, and work out how it got there.

• Pull it now. "At the end of the shift" is how it gets used by somebody who did not know.
• Check what is stored beside it. This is the step people skip, and it is the one that pays — one expired item is almost never one expired item. It is usually a delivery that got put away in front of the older stock.
• Ask why. If the answer is "we never rotate that shelf", you have just found next week's problem too.

Expired product is discarded. It does not get used up today because it is only just past.

questions.title: Put it in order, from the case arriving to the product leaving.
steps: Check the manufacturer's date on the case before you open anything
Fill the label in — made, ready and discard
Put it in the cooler behind what is already there, not in front of it
Check it on your daily walk through the walk-in
Pull it at close on the discard date
questions.explanation:
The two steps that get skipped are the fourth and the last.

• Checking the manufacturer's date BEFORE you open it is what stops you putting a seven-day label on something that expires in two.
• Putting it behind the older stock is the whole of rotation. Put it in front and the old product is now invisible, and it will still be there in three weeks.
• Pulling at close on the discard day is the one that turns into a morning deviation when nobody does it.

None of these takes extra time. They take doing it in this order.

questions.title: PHOTO: Go into your walk-in. Find the product that is CLOSEST to its date — or past it. Photograph the label so the date is readable.
questions.help: The closest one, not a tidy one. If something is already past date, that is the picture we want. Circle the date.

questions.title: PHOTO: Find an item that WE opened and date-marked ourselves. Photograph our label on it.
questions.help: If you cannot find a single opened item with our own date written on it, photograph the opened item that has no date. That is the finding, and it is worth knowing.

questions.title: How many items did you have to pull or re-label while taking this walk?
questions.help: Zero is a real answer. So is eleven. Your Area Coach would rather see the true number.

questions.title: What are you changing so this does not come back? Say who is doing it and when.
questions.help: Be specific. "Check dates daily" is not a plan. Who pulls dated product at close, and which shift checks the walk-in on the way in?
